## [§5.3.b] Trial with penalty — definition and logic

I call it a trial. with penalty. That sounds ugly. That's how I' call it internally. You wouldn't say that to somebody. But it's a trial with penalty. So basically, a customer can try out your product or service for free so long as they meet your terms. For comparison, the win-your-money-back offer, the attraction offer, gives customers the chance to get their money back if they meet the terms. In a trial with penalty offer, customers only pay if they don't meet the terms. So the win-your-money-back and the free trial with penalty are virtually the same offer; we're just changing when they pay and how they pay. So they'll mirror the actions and results that you used in win-your-money-back, but this time, we use avoiding fees rather than winning your money back as the incentive for adherence. So they avoid penalties rather than get or losing their money that they paid originally. All right, so with a trial with penalty, this isn't, "Here's my thing, see if you like it." It's, "Here's my thing. You get it for free so long as you do this stuff, which makes you a perfect fit for my next offer. And if you don't, then you have to pay for it." So it's kind of like a win-win for you, because if they don't do it, then they pay. And if they do do it, then they're gonna be really likely to buy the next thing. Now, I'm gonna give you something like, "Wait, so if they don't do it, then they pay, and they didn't wanna pay originally?" I'll cover how to get around that weirdness. Let's say you normally close three out of 10 people on your attraction offer, and now you downsell another four on a trial with penalty. Then, after the trial finishes, you upsell three of them. So you go from three sales to six sales, which doubles your customers. I use this as a downsell, but it could also be used as a front end. So I don't prefer to advertise this; I prefer to present this after someone already said no to giving me money. Some people advertise this as how they get customers. It's up to you. Obviously, that HR company advertised it as how they get customers. So if you really wanna help people, convincing them to put some skin in the game is a great way to do it. And so one of my sales rules is that everyone buys something who's qualified. And so I love that as a concept. It's like everyone should buy. Like, if they're qualified and we have the thing, every person should buy. The terms may change, but everyone should buy. So, here's the difference between trials and penalties and rebates. A trial is they j- you just get a card and then bill them later. A penalty/incentive is you get a card and bill later and also if they don't complete their activation activities. So the fees are associated with non-consumption and not showing up to other sales consultations. Remember the four things we had in the win-your-money-back is you wanna have them advertise your business, you wanna have them show up for sales consults, you wanna do things that, um, that get them results, and... There's another one. I can't remember what it was, but there's four, and those are the main ones. All right? So you want to associate them doing the things that gets them results, because if they get results, then they'll probably wanna buy. All right? So they're not here' for a trial; they're here to solve a problem, so solve it, because trials don't do anything. Them taking action is just what's going to solve their problem. This is just the easiest way that I can give you all this service for free. If you really do wanna do this, "I do wanna do this," great, then you're not gonna pay anything, 'cause you're gonna follow through, and this just gives you added incentive to do it. And if this doesn't work for you, then certainly nothing else will.

## [§5.3.f] Tweaking + naming + when to use vs pay-less-now

A couple other tidbits. So to tweak, tweak your trial to get the most customers. If no one takes your trial, lower the requirements or the priorities. If people take your trial but don't follow through, emphasize explaining how the fees help them, and make sure that you include meetings as mandatory. Like you have to highlight it. That's why I have the little separate lines for them to initial, and I walk through it with them. Don't let them read it. Explain each one, get them to nod, then initial. All right? If people don't stay on the back end, better emphasize the value of staying and paying. That's the early part where I said, "Hey, if we get you the results, would you stay?" We added that back in to our scripting when I saw my guys weren't doing it and we weren't getting as many ascensions. We added it back in, and then way more trials started ascending. Let people make up for goofs. So people often get discouraged after getting billed. But you can offer the opportunity to make it up. So this does a great job of getting people back on track and converting. But if they miss that, you're justified in billing them. So I don't see... Like if you, they miss something, you reach out, you reach out again. You say, "Hey, I'll make it..." You know, "I'll, I'll waive it, just come back in." If they miss the next one, it's up to you. I usually don't, but that, I just think that is a completely, you're completely justified in billing at that point. In terms of naming, just call it a trial. Just say, "We do it in a special way. And the way we do it gets people results rather than, than not results." That's pretty much it. So even though the trial with penalty has some special features, you should just call it a trial. Um, otherwise people may get scared or confused and no one wants to be penalized. All right? And if they ask you why you do free trials this way, just reply with, "It's how we've always done it." Pay less now, uh, or pay more later versus trial with penalty. So I use pay less now or pay more later as a downsell for physical products or one-time services. I use trial with penalty as a downsell for recurring products or services. Also, I've only made this work in businesses where the customer has to do work to get results. So if you find other types of businesses that this works for, these trials where they don't have to do anything, let me know. For the most part though, it's usually when somebody has to do something. Oftentimes like software, you usually have to do a lot of stuff in the software. Services, it's common for customers to have to do a bunch of stuff. Um, that's more, that's more normal.... discounts, uh, get card on file. So some people get weird when you offer free stuff and then ask for a card. And if you have a super low price, it justifies the card. So a small price, uh, means the card will probably work when automatic payments start. So instead of a free month, you might offer a firth month for a first month for a dollar, or then X dollars per month when it recurs. And so if you want, you can offer for a buck, a dollar down, $10 down, whatever, um, if you have a hard time with it. Anybody who has any acumen in sales should never have an issue closing a free trial with a card, personally. Rebates are a little tougher, uh, but they work the same way. You just get them to pay up front. So I consider rebates similar to win-your-money-back, but usually for smaller, like smaller in scope. So just get them to do the thing you need them to do, and then they get the rebate. So that was kind of like the, the story that I gave with, uh, Layla. So she paid, you know, 500 bucks. She had to attend two webinars or three webinars. Very clear, very small, very straightforward. That's where rebates are kind of nice, um, rather than, you know, billing. Because the thing is, is the rebate, you know the card works because you, they paid for it and then they get it rebated, which is basically a rollover onto their service afterwards. So those are the, uh, important points. Quick summary. In a trial with penalty offer, customers can try our product or service for free so long as they meet your terms. Trial with penalties, downsell offers get yeses from people who would have said no. To do them, you get the card, get the commitment, explain why they have to do it to get the results, the meetings they have to attend and what happens if they don't do it, and use the same refund criteria from your win-your-money-back, the attraction offer number one, to create your trial with penalty criteria. This way, at the end of the trial, they've done the stuff that makes a great tr- long-term customer, and they advertise your business for you. Breakup fees, you can charge by criteria or you can charge a lump fee. I like breaking them up. So you can either say, "It's $50 for each of these occurrences." Or you can just say, "If you mess up any of these, you pay the full boat." I prefer the small dings, because then people are like, "Oh, I missed one. Now I shouldn't even try," right? I don't like that. You make money by getting people results and turning them into customers, not nickel-and-diming them with fees. My personal opinion. So use mid-trial check-ins to make more offers. If they love it, give them more of what they love. If they have problems, swap it for what makes sense for them. If they aren't using it, offer the ability to make it up to avoid the fees. This style of trial converts as much or a much higher percentage on the back end, which is why I do them. It retains goodwill, because you actually look like you're trying to help, which you are, and you get agreement before explaining the fees, just as a quick reminder, 'cause it's super important. And you can always do a normal trial as a down-downsell and remove that. But at that point, I don't think that person really is... They're just trying to leave. Um, and remember, everyone buys something. That's free trials.

## [§5.3.c] Examples — B2C, B2B, therapy, fee weighting

So let's walk through some examples. So I'll do a B2C version, so a business to consumer, and then I'll do a B2B. So let's say you do a business to consumer offer, 28-day kick-that-habit blueprint, whatever, right? So you get the trial for free and avoid the penalty fee. You must... Or to get the trial for free and avoid the penalty fee, you must attend all your consulting calls, post your progress in the group once a week, journal daily in our app, and attend feedback sessions and transformation sessions, AKA the upsell opportunities. Business to business offer: five-day get your first five clients challenge. All right? To get the trial for free and avoid the penalty fee, you must send 100 outbound messages per day, report stats on the outbound messages, attend the daily training, post in the group daily once you've done the homework, attend your graduation call, which is the upsell opportunity. And so these look really similar to what the win-your-money-back ones were, because they are the same thing. Now, let's say you had a therapy business. So offer a free 28-day breakthrough therapy, free trial plus penalty. You're gonna need, uh, to do the homework before each session and show up. If you don't do the homework, you're not going to get the results that you want. And if you don't show up, obviously you're not gonna get better. This will give you an added incentive to get better faster. So we charge a $50 non-compliance fee for not doing the homework or not doing the session. If you don't do the homework, then we can't help you in the session. Fair enough? You just explain it, how it works. Now, in this 28-day thing, you can have all the fees add up to the exact same amount of money that you would have charged in a win-your-money-back. So if they have, call it 10 things they have to do over X period of time, and it's a $500 thing, then you charge $50 per thing. Now, if some things are more important than others, let's say sales consultations, then you can make those ones $100 or $150 and the other things 25. You wanna weight the prices based on the importance for you as a business and for them getting results.
